note: Machine-readable record of the sources behind the Why there scene and the figures quoted with it. SOURCES.md carries the same entries in prose, with the rest of the page's sources.

sources.title: Annual Resident Population Estimates for Metropolitan and Micropolitan Statistical Areas and Their Geographic Components, vintage 2025
sources.publisher: US Census Bureau, Population Estimates Program
sources.used_for: Which metropolitan statistical areas have a population of 1,000,000 or more. The POPESTIMATE2025 column of the CBSA total rows, excluding metropolitan divisions and county components: 387 metropolitan statistical areas, 56 of them at a million or more.

sources.status: Not currently quoted anywhere on the page. Kept as the counterpart to the Orange County load figure, which is still used by the bar-scale note and the sources line; delete it if the land area is not coming back.

sources.title: Electricity Consumption Dashboards
sources.value: 19,225 GWh a year, which is about 2.2 GW of average load (19,225 / 8,760)

sources.title: 2026 Global Data Center Outlook
sources.value: about four years, the US national average wait for a grid connection; 18 to 24 months to build the data center itself in most US markets
sources.used_for: The two numbers on the Why there headline view: "4 yrs" captioned "Wait for grid power (US average)", and "2 yrs" captioned "Build the data center", which is 18 to 24 months rounded to a whole year. Also the grey benchmark bar in Make Your Own Power, "Wait in the grid queue: US average, about 4 years", drawn at 48 months on the same scale as the two build times beside it.

as_cited_by.title: How Long Does It Take to Power a Data Center?
as_cited_by.note: Asked for as cited by EC&M. The article carrying these figures is in Electrical Contractor Magazine (ecmag.com), which is a different title from EC&M / Electrical Construction & Maintenance (ecmweb.com); no ecmweb.com page stating them was found, so the magazine that does state them is the one recorded. No verified deep link to the JLL report itself, so the publisher and report name are recorded rather than a guessed URL.
as_cited_by.quote_summary: While it varies by state, the national average wait time is four years, according to the 2026 JLL Global Data Center Outlook. Building the shell takes 18 to 24 months in most US markets.

sources.caveat: The two numbers are different clocks on one project: the build is construction time, and the wait is measured from the developer's interconnection request to the date the utility can deliver the contracted megawatts. They overlap in practice rather than running end to end, which is the point the view makes by putting them side by side.

sources.title: How Long Does It Take to Power a Data Center?
sources.value: large power transformers take two to four years from most manufacturers
sources.used_for: The second line of the card behind "4 yrs": "Bottleneck: equipment backlog, large power transformers take 2 to 4 years".
sources.note: Asked for as cited by EC&M. The article carrying these figures is in Electrical Contractor Magazine (ecmag.com), which is a different title from EC&M / Electrical Construction & Maintenance (ecmweb.com); no ecmweb.com page stating them was found, so the magazine that does state them is the one recorded.
sources.caveat: Other outlets put large units higher, commonly three to five years, and Wood Mackenzie's survey averages run 128 weeks for power transformers and 143 for generator step-up units. The page quotes the lower, more widely reported range and says "2 to 4 years".

sources.title: AI data centers, directory: OpenAI Stargate Abilene
sources.value: a 200 MW substation built in 2022 and expanded in 2024, enough to power both buildings; the larger 1 GW substation is not complete
sources.used_for: The first half of the Stargate Abilene card in Make Your Own Power: "Existing 200 MW substation".

sources.title: Behind-the-meter data centers, full report: Stargate Abilene
sources.value: on-site gas generation, with turbines ordered from GE Vernova in December 2024
sources.used_for: The second half of the same card: "plus an on-site gas plant; turbines ordered December 2024".
sources.caveat: Turbine counts differ by source: Cleanview lists a December 2024 order from GE Vernova and 5 LM2500XPRESS units installed alongside Solar Titan 350s, a 29-unit order is reported elsewhere, and permits at the site cover 10. Crusoe has said the turbines are for backup power despite permits allowing continuous use. The card claims the order date and the existence of on-site gas, not a count or a duty cycle.

sources.title: xAI begins removal of temporary gas turbines
sources.value: temporary gas turbines ran at Colossus until the MLGW substations were ready; removal began May 2025, with the rest staying until the second substation was finished
sources.used_for: The Colossus 1 card in Make Your Own Power: "Ran on temporary gas turbines until grid substations were ready".
sources.caveat: Simplified: the site also ran on Tesla Megapacks and some MLGW supply during that period, and the first substation came online in spring 2025, after the four months Epoch's dates cover. The claim is about what carried the site to first power, not that turbines were its only source.

sources.title: Alphabet Completes $4.75 Billion Acquisition of Intersect Power
sources.value: $4.75 billion in cash plus assumed debt, closed March 2026; the first announced co-located data center and power site is under construction in Haskell County, Texas
sources.used_for: The Haskell County marker card in Make Your Own Power, and the marker's existence.
sources.caveat: Intersect's existing operating assets in Texas and its California assets were not part of the acquisition, and Intersect continues to operate under its own brand.

sources.title: 2025 Gazetteer Files, counties
sources.value: Haskell County, Texas (GEOID 48207), internal point 33.175964, -99.730774, 903.133 sq mi of land
sources.used_for: Where the Haskell County marker is drawn. It is the county's internal point, not the site's location, which is why the card says the location is shown at county level.

sources.title: Q2 2026 earnings call transcript
sources.value: mostly sold out through 2030, and expecting more than half of the 30 GW of 2031 production slots to be under contract by the end of 2026
sources.used_for: The card behind the closing line of Make Your Own Power: "A large gas turbine ordered today arrives around 2031".
sources.caveat: This is an inference, not a quote. The company gave slot availability, not a delivery date: with 2030 largely sold, a new order lands in 2031 or later. The page says "around 2031" rather than naming a date. The call was also reported by trade outlets; the company's own transcript is cited here instead.

footnotes.text: 2 yrs, Build the data center / 4 yrs, Wait for grid power (US average)
footnotes.shown: The headline view of the Why there scene, as two numbers that count up from zero. The second one opens a card: "Waiting for: new generation, new high-voltage lines and substations" and "Bottleneck: equipment backlog, large power transformers take 2 to 4 years".
basis: Build: 18 to 24 months in most US markets, shown as 2 yrs (jll-time-to-power, as cited by Electrical Contractor Magazine).
Grid wait: about four years on US average, shown as 4 yrs (jll-time-to-power, JLL 2026 Global Data Center Outlook).
Transformers: two to four years from most manufacturers (ecm-transformer-lead-times).
footnotes.kind: elapsed time, rounded to whole years
footnotes.caveat: See the caveat on jll-time-to-power: the two clocks overlap rather than running end to end.
footnotes.replaces: time-to-power-bars, the three growing bars this view used to carry.

footnotes.text: Amazon New Carlisle: 16 months from start to first building live, vs about 4 years average grid wait
footnotes.shown: Step 5 of the Connect to the Grid view, with that site's bar picked out in white.
basis: 16 months: Epoch AI's own dates for Anthropic-Amazon New Carlisle, first dated observation 2024-02-09 to first operational 2025-06-23, which is 500 days or 16.4 months (data/sites.json).
About 4 years: the US average wait for a grid connection (jll-time-to-power).
footnotes.kind: elapsed time, on two different clocks
footnotes.caveat: See the caveat on jll-time-to-power. The 16 months is one site's build; the four years is the national average queue, so the line is a comparison of orders of magnitude rather than of two measurements of the same thing. New Carlisle sits 68.8 mi from Chicago, its nearest metro of a million or more, and broke ground in 2024.

footnotes.text: This group splits in two: seven sites within 53 mi, seven beyond 161 mi.
footnotes.shown: In the card a 2025-and-later site opens in the Connect to the Grid view, under its distance.
basis: Computed from data/metros.json: of the 14 sites that broke ground in 2025 or later, 7 are 12.2 to 52.5 mi from their nearest metro of a million or more and 7 are 161.0 to 288.7 mi, with nothing in between.
The group's median of 107 mi therefore falls in an empty gap, which is why a site in it carries this line.
footnotes.kind: distribution of the group behind the median

footnotes.text: Amazon New Carlisle, 2024: 16 months / Google Council Bluffs East, 2022: 26 months / Same grid, the right site cuts the wait
footnotes.shown: Step 6, the last of the Connect to the Grid view, with both sites picked out in white.
basis: Both rows are Epoch's own dates, first dated observation to first operational: New Carlisle 2024-02-09 to 2025-06-23, 500 days or 16.4 months; Council Bluffs East 2022-09-06 to 2024-11-19, 805 days or 26.4 months (data/sites.json).
Council Bluffs East sits 14 mi from Omaha, its nearest metro of a million or more; New Carlisle 68.8 mi from Chicago (data/metros.json).
footnotes.kind: elapsed time, both on Epoch's clock
footnotes.caveat: Unlike the earlier steps, this one compares like with like: two sites, the same measurement, the same source. What it cannot show is why, since the dates carry no reason for the gap.

footnotes.text: xAI Colossus 1: about 4 months, 35 MW live / Oracle Stargate Abilene: 16 months, 105 MW live / Wait in the grid queue: US average, about 4 years / Google + Intersect: no live date yet
footnotes.shown: The three steps of Make Your Own Power, as bars and as legend rows, each with a card behind it.
basis: Colossus 1: 2024-04-24 to 2024-08-11, 109 days or 3.6 months, shown as about 4 months, with 35.0 MW of IT power on the row where its first building came online (Epoch AI, data/sites.json, field it_mw_first_operational).
Stargate Abilene: 2024-05-31 to 2025-09-26, 483 days or 15.9 months, shown as 16 months, with 105.0 MW live on that row (Epoch AI, data/sites.json).
The grid queue benchmark: about four years, drawn at 48 months (jll-time-to-power).
Haskell County: no duration and no live date, because the site is under construction (cleary-intersect).
Bar lengths are those durations at one pixel scale and one speed, so a bar's length is the wait.
footnotes.kind: elapsed time, all on Epoch's clock
footnotes.caveat: The live figure is what was on the site's own first-operational row, not what it reached later: Colossus 1 was at 139 MW three weeks after its 35. The three examples are also not the same kind of thing, and the benchmark is a national average queue rather than a build, which is why it is grey and not a site.
